Period schedule:

Total: 5 periods · 3h 20min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.28): paired discussion — would experience differ without sight or hearing?
Let us discuss (p.31): identify true statements about Helen Keller's essay.

time_bands.activity: Open with the pair-discussion prompt from 'Let us read' (p.28): students briefly share whether a visit to a favourite place would change without sight or hearing. Take two or three responses aloud to surface the idea of sensory experience as the heart of memory.

Read the essay aloud, teacher-led, with students following in their textbooks (p.28–31). Pause at Keller's description of touching a leaf, a birch's smooth bark, and a singing bird to invite students to close their eyes and imagine the sensation.

Work through the 'Let us discuss' true-statement task (p.31) as a whole-class discussion. Read each statement aloud, ask students to vote, then press for the evidence in the text that confirms or refutes it.

periods.teacher_notes: Helen Keller's opening description of touch — the symmetry of a leaf, the quiver of a singing bird felt through a small tree — is the essay's emotional anchor; linger there so students feel the gap between her rich tactile world and the sight she imagines. Students often misread statement 2 (she observes suffering) as true; guide them to the full sentence where she also reads smiles and determination. Tasks not covered in class — the pre-reading sensory-details writing (p.28) — may be explored independently by interested students.

periods.activity_title: Three Days, Three Visions: Close Reading and Reflection

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.32): complete the three-day table of what Keller wished to see.
Let us think and reflect (p.32): Extract 1 — tone, texture phrases, and symbolism of leaf.
Let us think and reflect (p.33): two reflective questions on senses and the author's values.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.32): short answer — how does Keller understand a person's feelings without sight?

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs to complete the 'Let us discuss' three-day table (p.32), filling in what Keller plans for each day of sight. Pairs share their entries; the teacher builds a composite table on the board, correcting any conflation of Day 2 (dawn and museums) with Day 3 (the city corner).

Move to Extract 1 ('Let us think and reflect', p.32): read the extract aloud, then take the questions on the tone, the texture phrases, and what 'delicate symmetry of a leaf' symbolises. Students respond briefly in writing before a class share-out.

From 'Let us think and reflect' (p.33), take two open reflective questions: why does Keller believe sight is the most wonderful sense, and what her three-day choices reveal about her values and priorities. Students discuss in pairs, then two or three share with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read Keller's essay aloud and discussed the true-statement task, students now move into the analytical layer — what her choices reveal about her inner world. Watch for students who list museums for Day 1 or friends for Day 2; the day-by-day table is the correction point. The 'window of the soul' short-answer (p.32) is set as home reading so the reflective discussion in class is not rushed.

periods.activity_title: Listening to Inclusion, Speaking about the Senses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.36): select four true statements from the Anuj–mother conversation.
Let us speak (p.36): one-minute guided talk on the sense each student values most.

time_bands.activity: Set the listening context briefly: students will hear a conversation between a boy named Anuj and his mother about a new classmate, Braille, and digital inclusion. Ask students to keep the seven statements visible in their books (p.36) before the first reading.

Read the transcript aloud twice at natural pace — once for gist, once for detail. After the second reading, students individually mark the four statements they believe are true, then compare with a partner. Run a whole-class check, pressing students to cite the exact line that confirms or rules out each statement.

Move to 'Let us speak' (p.36): display or read the prompt-scaffold aloud. Give students a quiet minute to choose their sense and mentally frame their talk, then take turns in pairs for a quick exchange. Invite three or four students to speak briefly for the class, with the teacher modelling once if needed.

periods.teacher_notes: The conversation is rooted in the essay's theme of visual impairment and sensory experience, so the listening task naturally extends the reading rather than sitting apart from it. Students commonly mark statement 1 (Anuj finds Braille fascinating) as true; guide them to the mother's line about a 'right mindset' as the key to statement 7. For the speaking task, quieter students benefit from the pair exchange before whole-class sharing — the constitution's guidance on inclusive participation is especially relevant here.

periods.activity_title: Writing a Descriptive Paragraph: A Place through Five Senses

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.37): draft a three-part descriptive paragraph of a recently visited place.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the descriptive paragraph form using Keller's own writing as a mentor text: read one or two sentences from her sensory descriptions aloud and identify the three structural moves — an arresting opening, sensory supporting detail, and a concluding impression. Write the structure on the board.

Students spend a quiet planning phase: choose a place, jot three to five sensory images (one per sense where possible), and note one figure of speech — a simile, alliteration, or personification — they will include. The teacher circulates, prompting students who struggle to specify a concrete detail for at least two senses.

Students draft their paragraph independently, following the 'Let us write' guidelines (p.37). The teacher circulates and gives brief formative nudges — checking that the opening line is engaging, that at least three senses appear in the supporting lines, and that the final sentence creates a whole impression.

Students exchange drafts with a partner for a quick peer read: the partner underlines one strong sensory phrase and marks any place where a sense is missing or vague. Two or three students read their opening line aloud to the class.

periods.teacher_notes: Helen Keller's longing to see the world through five senses — discussed in earlier reading — gives students a vivid model of what sensory language does. The common weakness is a generic opening ('I visited a park') rather than an image that drops the reader into the scene; the mentor-text demonstration in the first band targets this directly. Drafting, peer response, and any revision are all completed within this sitting.

periods.activity_title: Modal Verbs, Sensory Words, and Braille Exploration

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.34): identify modal verbs and their functions in given sentences.
Let us learn (p.35): fill blanks with appropriate modal verbs for seven situations.
Let us explore (p.37–38): study the Braille code and write your name using tactile dots.

homework.task_brief: Let us explore (p.38): find out when and how India observes the International Day of Persons with Disabilities.

time_bands.activity: Introduce modal verbs using three or four sentences drawn from Keller's essay — her repeated use of 'should' to express imagined possibility is the entry point. Ask students why Keller writes 'I should see' rather than 'I will see', and write the function categories (possibility, necessity, moral obligation, ability, polite request) on the board.

Work through the 'Let us learn' modal identification task (p.34) orally as a class, then move immediately to the fill-in-the-blanks task (p.35). Students complete it individually, then pairs compare; the teacher checks answers focusing on the distinction between 'must' (obligation) and 'ought to' (moral obligation).

Shift to 'Let us explore' (p.37–38): the teacher displays or sketches the Braille grid on the board and explains the dot-cell system. Students use bindis, daal grains, or pencil dots on paper to encode their own name in Braille, then swap with a partner and try to decode it by touch or careful visual inspection.

periods.teacher_notes: Keller's use of 'should' throughout her three-day vision — expressing not obligation but imagined or wished-for possibility — gives modal verb instruction a live, meaning-rich anchor in this essay. Students often conflate 'can' (ability) with 'may' (permission); the fill-in task separates these in context. The sensory-words table (p.34, task index 0) is not covered in class; students who wish to extend their vocabulary work may complete it independently using the words from Keller's essay.
materials: Bindis, daal grains, or small stickers for the Braille activity

items.source_context: Helen Keller's three-day vision plan, sensory descriptions, tone, and her appeal to sighted readers.
items.item_stem:
Helen Keller imagines three days of sight and plans each day differently. Read the statements below and write True or False for each. Give one reason from the essay for each answer.
1. On the first day Keller would go to a museum to see the history of humankind.
2. On the second day Keller would arise with the dawn to witness night turning to day.
3. On the third day Keller would stand at a busy city corner to watch ordinary people.
4. Keller believes that touch alone satisfies all her longing for sensory experience.

options.text: On the first day Keller would go to a museum to see the history of humankind.
On the second day Keller would arise with the dawn to witness night turning to day.
On the third day Keller would stand at a busy city corner to watch ordinary people.
Keller believes that touch alone satisfies all her longing for sensory experience.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer:
1. False — Keller reserves museums for the second day, not the first; the first day is for seeing the people whose kindness has enriched her life.
2. True — She explicitly plans to arise with the dawn on the second day to witness the miracle of night turning to day.
3. True — On the third day she pictures herself at a busy city corner, reading smiles and suffering on the faces of passers-by.
4. False — Touch intensifies rather than satisfies her longing; she says 'so much beauty is available without sight', implying she believes vision reveals far more.

items.source_lo: Student reads and analyses an informational personal essay, identifying the author's perspective, evaluating textual claims, and interpreting literary choices using informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Helen Keller's three-day vision plan, sensory descriptions, tone, and her appeal to sighted readers.
items.item_stem: In the closing section of her essay, Helen Keller makes a passionate appeal to sighted readers, urging them to 'use your eyes as if tomorrow you might be struck blind.' What does this appeal reveal about Keller's perspective on how most sighted people treat the gift of vision? Support your answer with at least two specific details from the essay.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Keller's appeal reveals that she believes sighted people take vision for granted and fail to observe the world with genuine attention. She reinforces this by describing how she, who cannot see, can detect the beauty of a leaf's symmetry and a bird's quiver through touch alone — suggesting that those with sight miss even more. Her advice to apply the same urgency to all the other senses shows she views mindful sensory engagement as a deliberate choice, not a passive habit.

items.source_context: Anuj and his mother discuss Braille, Digital India, screen readers, and inclusive technology for the visually impaired.
items.item_stem:
Listen to the conversation between Anuj and his mother about Tara, Braille, and the Digital India initiative. Then choose the correct answer for each question.

1. When Anuj first sees the writing in Tara's books, what does he notice about it?
A. It uses pictures instead of letters.
B. It looks different and Tara tells him it is called Braille.
C. It is written in a language he does not recognise.
D. It is printed in very large letters for easy reading.

2. Anuj's first understanding of Digital India is that it is mainly about —
A. building more schools for the visually impaired.
B. providing free smartphones to all students.
C. learning how to use computers and being computer literate.
D. creating jobs in the banking sector.

options.label: Q1-A
options.text: It uses pictures instead of letters.

options.label: Q1-B
options.text: It looks different and Tara tells him it is called Braille.

options.label: Q1-C
options.text: It is written in a language he does not recognise.

options.label: Q1-D
options.text: It is printed in very large letters for easy reading.

options.label: Q2-A
options.text: Building more schools for the visually impaired.

options.label: Q2-B
options.text: Providing free smartphones to all students.

options.label: Q2-C
options.text: Learning how to use computers and being computer literate.

options.label: Q2-D
options.text: Creating jobs in the banking sector.

what_each_option_reveals.Q1-A: Suggests the student invented a visual detail not present in the transcript; Braille is tactile, not pictorial.
what_each_option_reveals.Q1-C: Confuses script unfamiliarity with a foreign language; the transcript names the script explicitly as Braille.
what_each_option_reveals.Q1-D: Conflates accessibility formats; large print is a different accommodation from Braille.
what_each_option_reveals.Q2-A: Draws on the general topic of inclusion but goes beyond what Anuj actually says in the conversation.
what_each_option_reveals.Q2-B: Extends the mother's point about smartphones into a give-away programme not mentioned in the transcript.
what_each_option_reveals.Q2-D: Repeats a detail the mother mentions as an outcome of Digital India, not Anuj's initial understanding of it.

items.source_context: Anuj and his mother discuss Braille, Digital India, screen readers, and inclusive technology for the visually impaired.
items.item_stem: Anuj's mother ends the conversation by saying, 'Remember, inclusion is not just about having the right tools, but also the right mindset.' Based on the conversation as a whole, explain in two to three sentences what you think she means by 'the right mindset', and give one example from the conversation that shows either Anuj or his mother demonstrating it.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: By 'the right mindset' the mother means an attitude of genuine openness and respect toward people with disabilities — not just providing them with assistive technology, but valuing their independence and participation. Anuj demonstrates this when he says he is proud of his school for having facilities for Tara, showing he sees inclusion as something worth celebrating rather than merely tolerating.

items.item_stem: Helen Keller describes how she experiences the world through touch — feeling the bark of trees, the quiver of a singing bird, and the warmth of sunshine. Think about the sense you value most in your own life. Describe a specific moment when that sense made an experience especially memorable for you. Use at least two vivid details in your response.

expected_elements: Names a specific sense and states clearly why it matters.
Describes a concrete personal moment linked to that sense.
Includes at least two vivid sensory details.
Speaks in connected sentences at an audible, steady pace.

items.item_stem: Keller closes her essay by urging sighted people to live as though they might lose their sight tomorrow. Do you agree that imagining the loss of a sense changes the way we value it? Share your opinion in a short talk, giving at least one reason and one real-life example to support your view.

expected_elements: States a clear opinion — agrees, disagrees, or qualifies the claim.
Gives at least one reasoned argument linking imagination of loss to appreciation.
Supports the argument with a real or hypothetical example.
Maintains an appropriate register — considered, not purely anecdotal.

items.item_stem: Write a descriptive paragraph about a market, garden, or public place you have visited. Your paragraph must have three clearly identifiable parts: (1) an opening line that drops the reader immediately into the scene, (2) supporting sentences that include at least three different senses — what you saw, heard, smelled, touched, or tasted — and one figure of speech such as a simile or personification, and (3) a closing sentence that leaves the reader with a single strong impression of the place.

expected_elements: Opening line places the reader in the scene immediately.
At least three distinct senses are named with specific detail.
One figure of speech — simile, alliteration, or personification — is used accurately.
Closing sentence creates a unified final impression, not just a summary.

items.source_context: Three-part descriptive paragraph of a visited place using sensory details and figures of speech.
items.item_stem: Helen Keller imagines what she would see on her first day of sight: the faces of friends whose kindness has shaped her life. Imagine you are writing to a younger student who has never tried to notice the world through more than one sense at a time. Write a short letter — with a proper greeting, body, and closing — in which you explain why paying attention to all five senses makes any experience richer. Draw on at least one specific idea from Keller's essay and at least one experience of your own.

expected_elements: Uses informal letter format — greeting, paragraphed body, closing sign-off.
Incorporates at least one specific idea from Keller's essay accurately.
Includes a personal experience that concretely illustrates multi-sensory attention.
Tone is friendly and encouraging, appropriate for a younger reader.

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies modal verbs in context, distinguishing the functions they express, using the language of the informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Modal verbs drawn from Keller's essay — possibility, necessity, moral obligation, ability, polite request — and fill-in practice.
items.item_stem: Match each sentence from or inspired by Helen Keller's essay in Column A with the function of the modal verb it contains in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A (Sentence)|Column B (Function of modal verb)
We ought to treasure every moment of sight we have.|moral obligation
She can detect broad emotions through the feel of a face.|ability
I should arise with the dawn on the second day.|possibility / imagined wish
You must use your eyes as if tomorrow you might be struck blind.|necessity
Might I borrow your textbook to read her essay, please?|polite request

answer_key.left: We ought to treasure every moment of sight we have.
She can detect broad emotions through the feel of a face.
I should arise with the dawn on the second day.
You must use your eyes as if tomorrow you might be struck blind.
Might I borrow your textbook to read her essay, please?

items.source_lo: Student identifies and applies modal verbs in context, distinguishing the functions they express, using the language of the informational text as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Modal verbs drawn from Keller's essay — possibility, necessity, moral obligation, ability, polite request — and fill-in practice.
items.item_stem:
The sentences below are inspired by the themes and language of Helen Keller's essay. Rewrite each sentence by replacing the underlined modal verb (given in parentheses) with a different modal verb that expresses the same function. Then write one sentence explaining how the meaning shifts — or does not shift — between your choice and the original.

(i) A sighted person (can) learn to see the world the way Helen Keller does — with gratitude and wonder. [function: ability]
(ii) We (should) pause each day and truly notice what our senses are telling us. [function: moral obligation / advice]

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (i) Acceptable replacements for 'can' expressing ability include 'is able to' or 'could' (in a more tentative register). A student might write: 'A sighted person could learn to see the world the way Helen Keller does — with gratitude and wonder.' The shift: 'could' introduces a slight sense of conditionality or lesser certainty compared with 'can', which states the ability as straightforwardly possible. (ii) Acceptable replacements for 'should' expressing moral obligation or advice include 'ought to' or 'must'. 'We ought to pause each day and truly notice what our senses are telling us.' 'Ought to' is slightly more formal and implies a stronger moral duty than 'should', which can sound like gentle advice.

items.source_context: Braille code, dot-cell writing system, and encoding one's name using tactile materials.
items.item_stem: Using the Braille code chart provided in your textbook (p.37–38), encode a short message of four to six words in Braille using dots on paper — you may press a pencil firmly, use bindis, or use daal grains. Then write two sentences explaining how this activity helped you understand what it might feel like to communicate without sight, drawing a connection to Helen Keller's experience as described in the essay.

expected_elements: Braille message is four to six words, dots placed with reference to the chart.
Reflection names a concrete difficulty noticed while encoding or decoding.
Connection to Keller's experience is specific — references touch as her primary sense.
Writing is in complete sentences and shows genuine engagement with the task.

items.item_stem: Design a one-page awareness poster for your classroom on the theme 'Inclusion Begins with Understanding'. Your poster must: (1) include the name and a one-sentence explanation of at least two assistive tools or practices that help people with visual or hearing impairment (such as Braille, screen readers, or sign language); (2) carry one central slogan of your own composition; and (3) include a short note — three to four sentences — explaining how Helen Keller's essay and the Braille activity in class influenced your design choices.

expected_elements: Names at least two assistive tools with accurate one-sentence explanations.
Slogan is original, concise, and thematically relevant to inclusion.
Reflective note makes a genuine, specific link to Keller's essay or the Braille activity.
Overall design is readable and audience-appropriate for a classroom display.
